lines.say: In the seventeen hundreds, Hanukkah coins weren't only for kids.
Across Eastern Europe, people gave them to religious teachers, as a thank you.
Some of those teachers traveled village to village to give lessons.
People paid them with what they had. Coins, food, honey, even whiskey.
By the eighteen hundreds, the coins had moved mostly to the children.
Then in the nineteen twenties, an American candy company wrapped chocolate coins in gold foil.
The chocolate stuck around. The thank you is easy to forget.
Your regulars showed up for you all year. Did you reach back?
